The low cost for tickets allows you to spend hours on this living history museum to see how the Navy spent their time on this floating city. You dont realize how big this ship is until you're in it and on top of the deck. We'll worth the time if you're in the area and you will love it.

I spent the last two days in Camden and it truly amazing experience. The ship was in a perfect state, testament to all the curatorial, general staff & volunteers. All of them help provide an amazing experience. Several members took the time to have conversations, suggestions & were extremely kind & respectful. The one negative I had was I did not meet curator Ryan Szimanski (who worked himself sick from the Navy’s 250th ceremonies ) which is testament to how hard he leads & works the entire team. My 9 year old has a bucket list to visit every battleship museum in the US. This is our 3rd battleship museum and it did not disappoint. It was a nice day and very few people were visiting the museum maybe because of the retirement ceremony being held. It was nice to hear over the loud speaker all the high ranking members of the armed forces that boarded the ship while we were touring. Many veterans were on board to  share their experiences and tell stories of their time at sea in the ship. Amazing educational experience. My son said it was the best birthday.

A must visit for anyone interested in naval history and American military history. I took the 2 hour guided tour and spent 4 hours walking around and exploring the ship and still feel like I only saw half of it. museums.content_summary: Step aboard the **Battleship New Jersey Museum & Memorial** and journey through over 80 years of naval history on this majestic floating museum. Explore the life of sailors who served, witness historic battles, and gain insights into the power of the U.S. Navy. This is more than just a museum; it’s an immersive experience that connects visitors with America's military legacy.
museums.content_description:
**Battleship New Jersey Museum & Memorial** serves as a tribute to those who served on this iconic vessel, the most decorated battleship in American history. As you walk the decks of this grand ship, you'll discover an authentic military environment where history comes alive. From the impressive **naval architecture** of the ship, which stretches over 900 feet long, to the detailed exhibits showcasing life at sea, each area of the battleship offers a unique glimpse into the past. The vessel has undergone numerous renovations, ensuring it provides a safe yet evocative experience for all who visit.  

Visitors will find engaging exhibits like the **captain's cabin**, which allows you to step into the shoes of those who commanded this massive ship, and the **fire control and command center**, where you can learn about the tactical operations of a battleship. Every corner of the New Jersey holds stories of bravery and valor—interactive displays and guided tours add layers to your understanding of naval warfare and maritime history.

One of the highlights is the opportunity to explore the **gun turrets** and even take a seat in the historical **FTS-1 fire control radar** room, providing hands-on experiences that bring the technical prowess of naval artillery to life. The tours are designed not just for history buffs but also for families, ensuring that visitors of all ages can appreciate the significance of this floating museum. With waterfront views of Philadelphia's skyline and the Delaware River, your visit to the **Battleship New Jersey** is both an educational and scenic experience that is bound to leave a lasting impression.
content_highlights: The most decorated battleship in U.S. history
Explore authentic naval architecture and design
Hands-on experiences in the gun turrets and command center
Engaging tours led by knowledgeable guides
Scenic views of Philadelphia from the battleship's decks

Nestled in the heart of Morris County, this charming museum was once the home of George Macculloch, a prominent figure in New Jersey’s industrial history. The museum itself is an architectural gem, featuring the elegant Federal-style design that reflects the sophisticated aesthetic of its time. As you step through the home, you’ll find period rooms lavishly restored, showcasing life during the early 1800s, complete with original furnishings and artwork that transport you back in time.  

One of the museum's standout features is its collection of American art, particularly works that highlight the Hudson River School movement, known for its lush landscapes and captivating depictions of the American wilderness. Visitors can also stroll through the beautifully landscaped gardens, designed in the early 20th century, which provide a peaceful retreat and a perfect backdrop for enjoying art-related events and seasonal programs. Guided tours are available, offering in-depth knowledge about both the historical context of the house and the significance of its collections, enhancing your visitor experience. The **Macculloch Hall Historical Museum** is not just a step into history; it's an interactive exploration of culture, art, and the past that should not be missed.

Stunning Federal-style architecture
Collection of Hudson River School artwork

google_reviews.text: Amazing historical house museum with many interesting artifacts showing the stories of the generations of people who lived there. The museum gives guided tours and has touchable artifacts and textured art for the visually impaired or for anyone who wants to touch a piece of history. The gardens are absolutely gorgeous and a very restful place to explore.

The staff are knowledgeable and patient and they gave us a careful tour even though my wife and I were the only two people there on a chilly day. Excellent way to spend a Sunday afternoon.  Rich history with changing exhibits and a knowledgeable staff. Accessibility seems to be an important goal of thiers with several options for people with different needs. Grateful to have gems like this to preserve history in Morristown.

museums.content_summary: Set in a leafy New Jersey suburb, the Montclair Art Museum rewards art lovers with a focused, thoughtfully curated encounter rather than an overwhelming marathon. Come for standout strengths in American art and a serious commitment to Native American works—an unusually rich focus for a regional museum. The galleries are calm and approachable, making it easy to look closely, connect movements to real objects, and leave feeling you’ve actually seen art. It’s a satisfying half-day museum visit with real connoisseur appeal.
museums.content_description:
**Montclair Art Museum** is the kind of regional museum that art enthusiasts quietly love: compact, carefully edited, and confident about its identity. Rather than trying to be encyclopedic, it leans into key American stories—works that trace the evolution of American painting and sculpture across the 19th and 20th centuries, with special attention to the ways *modernism* reshaped what “American art” could look like. For travelers, that means you can move from gallery to gallery with a clear sense of narrative, and spend your time *looking* instead of navigating crowds.

A major distinction is the museum’s commitment to Native American art, presented not as an add-on but as a core strength. Expect exhibitions that foreground materials, process, and cultural context—an approach that can sharpen your eye for form and symbolism no matter your collecting interests. The experience is intimate and study-friendly: good sightlines, manageable room sequences, and the feeling that each object has been selected to carry weight.

Architecturally, **Montclair Art Museum** reads as a dignified civic landmark—an inviting, human-scaled building that suits its role as a community anchor and makes for an easy, unhurried visit. Plan to linger with rotating shows, then enjoy Montclair’s walkable streets and cafés nearby; it’s an art outing that feels both restorative and intellectually satisfying.
content_highlights: Strong focus on American art, with an emphasis on 19th–20th-century developments and modernist shifts
Notable commitment to Native American art, often presented with depth and cultural context
A calm, close-looking gallery experience—ideal for art lovers who prefer quality over quantity
Rotating exhibitions that keep repeat visits rewarding even with a modest permanent collection
A dignified, civic-minded building in a walkable Montclair setting—easy to pair with a day in town

google_reviews.text: We had a fabulous experience hosting our wedding at the Montclair Art Museum. We mostly worked with Meryl, who took over running weddings at the MAM last year. She was incredibly responsive, attentive, and communicative throughout the process, providing true caring and enthusiasm for our wedding. While the MAM is a “load-in” venue, they have an excellent sound system, kitchens for catering staff to work from, and incredible lighting that makes the room stunningly romantic during the ceremony and fun during the reception. Guests LOVED being able to browse the museum as part of the cocktail hour, and Leir Hall is a truly beautiful room. For a wedding with many disabled guests including the bride and her mom, we were very impressed from day one with how accessible the venue is compared to others that we saw. While there is room for improvement, there was a lot of care and support with accessibility (including having a great, dedicated accessibility professional at the museum). Some words of advice for future married couples: one thing to be mindful of in planning your wedding here is some of the needs that relate to protecting the artwork, like only serving clear liquid in Lehman Court or requiring vendors be a certain distance from the wall to keep art safe - not a problem, just a consideration with what drinks you serve. And given the complexity of loading in various vendors, we definitely benefitted significantly from having a caterer who is used to working there (Cheryl from Church Street Catering) and a day-of coordinator to help keep everyone in sync. In conclusion, Meryl and the team really went above and beyond many times, from helping to plan out every aspect of the day to helping with many needs throughout the day. I highly recommend the MAM, it is a beautiful place that made for a truly incredible wedding.

Located on South Mountain Avenue in Montclair, New Jersey, the Montclair Art Museum is an absolutely beautiful space to enjoy an abundance of collections + art showcases. Per their website, "The Montclair Art Museum collects, exhibits, preserves, and interprets American and Native American art, honoring the creative accomplishments of a diverse range of artists, past and present."

I recently visited for the first time to attend a wedding that was being held within the museum's event space, and it was absolutely beautiful. The gallery spaces were lovely to view & enjoy during the event in themselves (particularly as these were accessible during the initial cocktail hour), but their designated event space for the reception itself was clean, well-kept, and was the perfect size to accommodate a dance floor, many tables & chairs, and a DJ booth!! Small but exquisite collection. When I visited they had no less than four artworks by John Singer Sargent (1856-1925), my favorite artist, on display. Also nice artworks by Elizabeth Catlett, Nan Goldin, Larry Sultan, Troy Jones, and Dread Scott. Also great museum store. I was slightly disappointed that no art by Morgan Russell (1886-1953) was on display but I hope that changes in future rotations of the permanent collection. Morgan Russell is currently prominently featured in the "Orphism" exhibition at the Guggenheim Museum. The Montclair Art Museum held a retrospective on Morgan Russell in 1990 for which I was fortunate to find the monograph at a local antique store.

Housed in the *historic Acorn Hall*, a stunning Greek Revival mansion built in 1853, the museum itself is a fascinating piece of architecture that offers insight into the local historical context. Visitors are welcomed into beautifully curated spaces where the past comes alive through an array of artifacts, docents’ stories, and interactive displays that highlight the everyday lives of past residents. Each visit provides an opportunity to delve into the unique stories that give Morristown its character and charm.  

The museum's collection is particularly noteworthy, showcasing everything from 19th-century costumes and period furniture to documents and photographs that chronicle the evolution of Morris County. Special exhibitions often focus on themes such as the Revolutionary War, local industries, and cultural shifts that resonate within the community. Additionally, the Annual Morristown History & Heritage Festival is a highlight for many, celebrating the area's diverse historical influences and inviting visitors to participate in reenactments, workshops, and family-friendly activities. Whether you're a history enthusiast or just looking to enjoy an afternoon learning about local culture, **Morris County Historical Society** provides a warm and enriching experience suited for all ages.

Extensive collection of 19th-century costumes
Unique documents and photographs documenting local history
Interactive exhibits focusing on Revolutionary War history

A Must-Visit Gem in Newark — The Newark Museum of Art! 🎨✨

So, my cousin called me on a random weekday asking if I could do her a favor — be the auntie-on-duty and chaperone my niece’s school field trip since the parents weren’t available. I checked my calendar, saw a free day, and immediately said, “Yes, I’m in!”

Come Wednesday morning, I met my niece at her school, hopped on the school bus with the students, and off we went to The Newark Museum of Art around 9 a.m. Everything was impressively organized — from check-in to the tour itself. The museum staff and tour guides were friendly, knowledgeable, and passionate about art and history. They walked us through each section, explaining the cultural background, artistic value, and historical stories behind every exhibit. I genuinely learned so much and gained a deeper appreciation for both global and local art.

As someone who loves visiting art museums, I was amazed to see familiar pieces I’d once seen at the Atlanta Art Museum — right here in New Jersey! It’s like art finds a way to connect us wherever we go.

The museum is very accessible and family-friendly. Parking was convenient, ramps and facilities were well-designed for visitors with disabilities, and all directions were clearly provided. Just a tip: book your tickets in advance, especially if you’re coming as a group of 10 or more. It saves you time and ensures a smooth experience.

Due to privacy and safety, I didn’t take many photos inside since I was focused on keeping the kids safe, but trust me — the visuals, the vibe, and the educational experience are unforgettable.

If you haven’t been, find time to visit The Newark Museum of Art. It’s a great opportunity to immerse yourself in art, culture, and history — and to truly understand the stories behind each masterpiece. Whether you’re a parent, educator, or just an art lover like me, this place is absolutely worth it!

💡 Highly recommended for school trips, families, or anyone looking to reconnect with creativity and culture right here in Newark.

Nice museum. The preservation of the Ballantine house as part of the museum is an interesting way to combine and preserve the historic house. The detailed woodwork was great to see. On the top floor of the museum there was also a piece from George Nakashima. I have seen pictures of his work before but it was the first time I saw one in person.  The planetarium was unfortunately closed when I visited. I also really liked the colorful glassware.

With a few hours to spare before leaving Newark, I slipped into the Museum of Contemporary Art—and it turned out to be time exceptionally well spent. I meandered from gallery to gallery, first soaking in bold American contemporary works, then unexpectedly pausing before early Mediterranean artifacts. In another space, a wall of 19th-century slave advertisements confronted me with the stark reality of people bought and sold little more than a century ago—an arresting reminder of history’s proximity. One room dazzled with explosions of color; the next offered a contemplative display of African art. In the span of a short visit, the museum delivered a remarkable breadth of art and emotion, transforming a quick stop into a far richer journey.

This is a great museum. It has three floors and a lot of different exhibits like native artists of North America innovators of the southwestern jewelry, the ballantin house,  art of global Asia, Tibetan alters, Buddhist, and many more. They do have a small eatery. I didn't try it. I instead went outside to eat and then returned to finish the museum.  The planetarium doesn't open until late November so I will be going back to check it out. I payed 10.60 with a student discount, if not it's 12 something. Overall, it's a great place to visit, catch up on history and see things from all over the world. It's also cute for kids because they have interactive activities for them.

google_reviews.text: The building inside is so beautiful! So comfy and grand. I love the interior design. And there are a lot of chairs and branches if you need to sit down. Restaurant on 3rd floor, didn’t try yet. A lot of interesting art collections. And it’s free admission!

I came here today to see the new building by David Adjaye (born 1966). It's a lovely museum that works well. The inside reminded me strongly of Louis Kahn's Yale Center for British Art, especially in terms of the ceilings and the use of light-colored wood. Some Miesian influence can be detected as well, especially at one of the inner courtyards. The outside is fairly neutral and does not take away from the historic campus buildings around it. The collection is great, ranging from antiquity to modern art. Some of my favorite artworks include works by Max Beckmann (a late work from 1950), Lucas Cranach the Elder, Dante Gabriel Rossetti, Frank Stella, Joan Mitchell, and Gerhard Richter, to mention just a few. I also like the way artworks from different periods, regions, and styles are juxtaposed. Lovely restaurant (mosaic) on the 3rd floor. Free entrance!

Beautiful art pieces. Two levels of unique and wonderful art in a peaceful and well appointed  setting.   Lovely  gift shop and a cafe on the third level. Impressive collections with amazing pieces. We found the entire visit and experience relaxing and so enjoyable.  We also enjoyed there was no entrance fee to experience all this beauty . Well worth a visit.

Excellent place for art and culture lovers.

The Princeton University Art Museum offers an impressive collection of artworks spanning different cultures and time periods. The exhibits are well curated, informative, and thoughtfully displayed, making the visit both engaging and educational.

The museum has a calm and elegant atmosphere, and the layout makes it easy to explore. It’s a wonderful place to spend a few hours on the Princeton campus and a must-visit for anyone interested in art and history.

Each gallery showcased curated pieces that spans centuries and continents. A few pieces rivals those in world renowned museums in UK, France, Italy, and Spain.
The 3.5 hours including a healthy brunch at the 3rd floor Mosaic restaurant was an enriching educational experience. PUAM is a must visit for novice and seasoned art enthusiasts.

Housed in a historic stone-and-timber mill complex, it’s a rewarding stop for travelers who enjoy seeing modern and regional creativity in an intimate setting. Expect rotating exhibitions, strong ties to working artists, and a visit that feels both cultural and restorative—easy to combine with strolling Clinton’s scenic bridges, shops, and cafés.
museums.content_description:
**Hunterdon Art Museum** in Clinton offers an art-lover’s kind of discovery: a **local museum with a contemporary pulse** set within one of New Jersey’s most photogenic small towns. Its strength is not vast encyclopedic holdings, but **thoughtful, well-edited exhibitions** that bring you close to the work—often spotlighting living artists, regional voices, and current conversations in *contemporary* practice. With a competent curatorial approach and frequent rotation, repeat visits are rewarded; you’re likely to encounter fresh perspectives across painting, photography, printmaking, and mixed-media approaches rather than a static “greatest hits” presentation.

Equally compelling is the setting. The museum’s identity is intertwined with Clinton’s historic riverside character, where **19th-century mill architecture**—rugged masonry, industrial proportions, and the tactile presence of old materials—creates a dramatic frame for modern art. That contrast can heighten your experience: crisp contemporary surfaces against weathered stone, quiet gallery moments balanced by the sense of a working past.

For travelers planning a museum day, the experience is pleasantly unhurried and human-scaled. You can take time with individual pieces, chat with staff, and then step outside to enjoy the town’s scenic views and walkable streets—making the museum an ideal anchor for a half-day itinerary centered on art, architecture, and atmosphere.
content_highlights: Contemporary-focused rotating exhibitions that keep the galleries feeling new
Intimate scale that encourages close looking and repeat visits
Historic mill-era architecture that adds texture and drama to the art experience
A strong sense of place in scenic Clinton—easy to pair with a town stroll and photos
A traveler-friendly stop for art enthusiasts seeking regional creativity over blockbuster crowds

google_reviews.text: A beautiful museum in a great setting. Our weekday visit was very smooth, with a wait time of under 10 minutes to enter. The exhibits are thought-provoking and the building itself is charming. Definitely worth a 4-star visit!
This a small art museum that changes exhibits frequently. The staff is friendly and helpful. We enjoyed the art that was featured during our visit. I hope to go back again next time I am in the area.

A worthwhile experience that is absolutely enlightening, intriguing, & astounding! I was impressed with the age of the building & how it was reconfigured into an art museum which must have been painstakingly difficult considering it was originally constructed in the 1800's! The grounds are breathtaking especially when the weather is nice! The receptionist was delightfully conversable & friendly to bat!

Hunterdon Art Museum is part of Bank of America's Museum On Us program. It's a perfect stop for us on our way back to PA after a weekend in NYC. It's right off I78, less than a mile from the Clinton exit.

As soon as we drove across the single lane historical bridge, we were already engrossed by the picturesque view of the red mill, the dam, and the stone museum building all within one view on the left. The main street at the other end of the bridge has the typical small town feel, lined with many charming boutiques and shops.  Street parking were all taken and we had to resort to the second municipal parking lot on the other side of the river, but still it was a manageable 1/4 mile walk to the museum.

The museum itself is quite small, especially the ground floor where the lobby and the children's craft room take up most of the space. Cristina de Gennaro's drawings about sage roots occupied the only gallery on the ground floor. The second floor was a special exhibit from Tricia Zimic with her porcelain sculptures using monkeys to depict themes of sins and virtues.  The third floor housed some of the art works by students and faculties.

The sweet short tour in the museum, coupled with the scenic surroundings and the quaint town make this stop well worth our time.
We enjoyed the Día de los muertos street fair. Not big but fun to stop in.  It's such a great location. The museum has some beautiful pieces.
